clue.text: Pet's loud greeting

blocks.note: f is the musician's mark for forte, the instruction to play loudly
ave is the Latin hail, the greeting of Ave Maria and Ave Caesar

explanation.surface: A dog barking its hello at the door.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing on the surface is about volume or Latin: an animal greets you noisily and that is the whole picture. The apostrophe-s is doing the work of an equals sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A fave is a favourite, and a pet — the teacher's pet, a pet project — is the one singled out for favour.

clue.text: The whiffler mostly daft, useless individual

indicators.note: Mostly is all but the last bit, so the words before it are written out one letter short at the end.
Somebody daft is not thinking straight, and letters in that condition do not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: eleven letters there, and dropping the final R leaves exactly the ten the grid wants

explanation.surface: A parade official written off as half-witted and surplus to requirements.
explanation.walkthrough: A whiffler is the man who clears a path in front of a procession, a job with the air of being unnecessary, so the surface reads as an insult rather than as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A cart runs on four wheels, so a fifth is along for the ride — the phrase means the person nobody in the group actually needs.

clue.text: That's all you have to say?

definitions.text: That's all you have to say?

blocks.note: the surface reading is a snub: is that really the whole of your argument, is that everything you can offer
the setter's reading counts words rather than weighing them — every one you own and can produce

explanation.surface: One person cutting another short for making a thin case.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'have to' as an obligation and the clue is a put-down; read it as possession and it is an inventory of every word you keep.
explanation.definitionFit: Your vocabulary is the whole stock of words at your disposal, so it literally is all you have to say.

clue.text: Slightly spoil drink put before friend

indicators.note: To put one thing before another is to set it in front, so the two chunks just clued go ahead of the word that follows.

blocks.note: to mar something is to spoil it, the way a scratch mars a table
gin is the crossword's default spirit, three letters and always to hand
an ally is the friend who is on your side in a fight

explanation.surface: A spoiled drink set down in front of a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slightly spoil' reads as one phrase, and only the first word of it is the definition — the spoiling belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Marginally means by a margin so small it barely counts, which is the job 'slightly' does in front of a verb.

clue.text: Converted layman suppresses expression of wonder, showing inconsistency

indicators.note: A converted building is one made over into something else, and letters made over the same way come back in a different order.
To suppress a cry is to hold it down out of sight, so the exclamation goes inside the letters rather than beside them.

blocks.note: the six letters of the noun rearranged, with a gap left after the second
the wondering exclamation written down is a single letter: O, look at that

explanation.surface: A new convert holding back a gasp of amazement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing inconsistency' looks like a participle rounding off the sentence, and it is the definition: one word of it, with 'showing' doing nothing but joining.
explanation.definitionFit: An anomaly is the one case that will not fit the pattern, which is inconsistency showing up in a single instance.

clue.text: Weapon's warm: has this been discharged?

definitions.text: Weapon's warm: has this been discharged?

blocks.note: the weapon is a gun, and the possessive apostrophe hands over its S as well
hot is warm taken a good deal further

explanation.surface: A detective at the scene, touching the barrel and drawing the obvious conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon is a dramatic pause on the surface and a joint in the wordplay. The whole sentence works as the definition too, which is what makes 'this' fair — it points at the answer rather than at the gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunshot is the round a firearm discharges, and a barrel still warm is the sign that one has just gone off.

clue.text: I've not saying I've done my run after workout

definitions.note: The definition describes the stance where the answer is the retort that takes it, and the clue prints 'I've not saying', which reads as a slip for 'I'm not saying'.

indicators.note: A workout leaves whatever goes through it thoroughly shaken up, and 'after' puts that treatment on the words in front of it.

blocks.note: the pronoun the printed clue puts in front of the definition, where the phrase wants 'I'm'; it hands over no letters
twelve letters in that boast, exactly the twelve the three words of the entry need

explanation.surface: A gym-goer insisting, a little defensively, that the run is already done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workout' is the sort of everyday noun a setter can bury an instruction in, and nothing in the sentence points at it. The clue says 'I've' twice, and only the second one is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Never you mind' is the phrase you use to shut a question down, which is what somebody who is not saying is doing.

clue.text: God, that's almost flipping funny

indicators.note: Almost there means stopping just short, so the word it governs gives up its final letter.
To flip a thing is to turn it over end for end, so the letters are read back the other way; the mild swearing is for the surface.

blocks.note: something funny is droll, and that word is written one letter short of its end

explanation.surface: Somebody half-amused, swearing mildly at a joke that nearly works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God' opens the clue as an oath and is doing duty as the definition, while 'flipping' reads as the same kind of mild swearing. Both words are working harder than they look.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord is God in Christian usage — the ordinary English title the Bible and the prayer book use for him.

clue.text: We're told the solver's going to festival

indicators.note: What we are told reaches us as sound, so what goes in the grid is spelt quite differently from the words that produce it.

blocks.note: the person solving the clue is 'you', and 'you will' contracts to one syllable

explanation.surface: Word has got round that whoever is doing the crossword is off to a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The solver' is the one phrase in the clue pointing out of the puzzle at the reader, and 'going to' is the future tense rather than a direction of travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Yule is the old name for the midwinter feast, kept alive in yule log and yuletide — Christmas under its pre-Christian name.

clue.text: Falsehood's absolute converse; truth, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily means at the start, so each word it governs gives up its opening letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: its opening letter; a falsehood is a lie
its opening letter; absolute means complete, with nothing held back
its opening letter; the converse of a thing is its opposite
its opening letter, taken like the three before it

explanation.surface: Someone explaining, a shade pompously, what the opposite of a lie is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Truth' looks like the definition parked at the end, and it is really the fourth word being mined for its initial. The sentence describes what its own initials spell, which is what the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: A fact is what is true rather than false, so read straight the sentence defines it: the exact opposite of a falsehood.

clue.text: Popular online: dubiously 'original', vacuous vlogging

definitions.note: The definition is adjectival where the answer is a verb phrase: something going viral is on its way to being popular online rather than already so.

indicators.note: Something done dubiously will not stand inspection, and letters handled that way do not come back in the order they went in.
A vacuous word is an empty one, so all that survives of it is the outside, the middle having gone.

blocks.note: the word in quotation marks is here for its eight letters, not for its meaning
the letters at the two ends of the word, with everything between them emptied out

explanation.surface: A vlogger's claim to be original is treated with suspicion and the content dismissed as hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'original' do two jobs at once: sneering at the vlogger on the surface, and marking the word off as raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Something going viral is passed from share to share until everyone online has seen it, which is how a thing becomes popular there.

clue.text: Part of bedtime routine: depict nursery-rhyme mice?

blocks.note: to draw something is to depict it in pencil or ink
the rhyme counts three of them and says in its title what is wrong with all three

explanation.surface: Bedtime asks for one more thing: a quick sketch of the mice from the rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three Blind Mice' is the rhyme, and the setter takes only the adjective from it — the number and the animals stay behind. The question mark admits you have to name the rhyme before you can borrow from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling the blind down across the window is one of the small jobs that shuts the day down, so it belongs to the bedtime routine.

clue.text: Sewer's outlet?

blocks.note: read as the drain under the street, which is what the surface is about, and the word is said quite differently in that sense
an outlet is also a shop, so the question is where somebody at a sewing machine goes for thread, buttons and zips

explanation.surface: A question about where the drains empty out.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke rests on one word with two pronunciations: the drain, and the person who sews. British high streets kept these shops for the small-wares a dressmaker needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A haberdasher sells sewing small-wares, so anybody who sews buys there — 'outlet' in the retail sense rather than the plumbing one.

clue.text: Avoid having charged description of Drake?

blocks.note: to duck a punch or a question is to avoid it
a customer who was charged for something was billed for it

explanation.surface: Keeping clear of a highly charged account of Drake.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital D pulls hard towards Sir Francis, or towards the rapper, and the setter means neither: a drake is a male duck.
explanation.definitionFit: A drake is a male duck, so the compound describes him exactly — the question mark owns up to using a zoologist's word for an ordinary bird.

clue.text: Flighty type giving crockery to nitwit

blocks.note: china is the fine white ware a crockery cupboard is full of, named after the country that first exported it
a silly goose is an old and gentle way of calling somebody a nitwit

explanation.surface: A frivolous sort handing plates over to an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty type' wants to be a scatty person and means a bird that flies. The breed is the big farmyard goose developed from the Asian swan goose, known for the knob above its bill.
explanation.definitionFit: The China goose is a domestic breed of the swan goose, so it is one particular flying bird — 'flighty type' read literally.

clue.text: At midpoint of entrance area, having change of heart

indicators.note: Somebody who has a change of heart swaps what sits at their centre for something else, and the heart of a seven-letter word is the letter in the middle of it.

blocks.note: a hallway is the strip of floor you step onto from the front door, the area the entrance opens into

explanation.surface: Somebody stops in the middle of the hall, thinks better of it and turns back.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here says which letter arrives: the heart of the entrance area is an L, and the crossings tell you an F replaces it. On the surface 'change of heart' is somebody relenting, not a middle letter being swapped.
explanation.definitionFit: Halfway is where you stand when half the distance is behind you and half in front, which is the midpoint of anything you can travel along.

clue.text: Meditator's sound, in a sense, is more than is tolerable

indicators.note: The plainest insertion signal there is: what has just been named goes inside whatever is named next.

blocks.note: touch is one of the five senses, and its five letters open up to take a passenger
om is the syllable chanted in meditation, hummed on one long note

explanation.surface: A complaint that the chanting next door has gone beyond what anybody can stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a sense' is the phrase people use for 'loosely speaking', which is exactly what it is not doing here: the sense is one of the five, and it is wanted for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Too much is the point past which a thing stops being bearable, so 'more than is tolerable' is the plain measure of it.

clue.text: Most of the lining primitive material

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it but the last letter, so the final one is never written down.
A lining sits inside the coat, so the letters it governs go within the other word rather than alongside it.

blocks.note: primitive man is early man, the first and simplest of his kind
the definite article with its last letter left off

explanation.surface: The bulk of a garment's lining turns out to be crude stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing announces itself as an instruction: 'lining' is a noun on the surface and a verb in the wordplay. 'Material' is the philosopher's sense, the opposite of spiritual, not a bolt of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthly means belonging to this world rather than the next, which is the sense 'material' carries in earthly goods and material comforts.

clue.text: Former president in style, fashionable

indicators.note: Buried in 'fashionable' is the verb fashion — to shape a thing into a new form — and letters being shaped end up in a new order.

blocks.note: seven letters in that phrase, exactly the seven the entry wants and no others

explanation.surface: Somebody arriving in style and thoroughly in vogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In style' looks like the manner of the great man's arrival and is the raw material; the only instruction in the clue is the last word, dressed as a compliment.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Yeltsin was Russia's first president, in office through the 1990s, so he is one particular former holder of the job.

clue.text: Protuberance on monarch, largely unsophisticated type

indicators.note: Largely means the greater part of a thing, so the word keeps all of itself except the final letter.

blocks.note: a bump is a small protuberance, the lump a knock leaves behind
a monarch is a king, and the greater part of that word is its first three letters

explanation.surface: A swelling raised on the royal head.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means no more than 'next to', so the two pieces are laid left to right in the order they are clued rather than one above the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumpkin is a countryman held to be too rustic to know how to behave in town, so the insult is exactly 'unsophisticated type'.

clue.text: Bare mud wrestling in Atlantic tourist destination

indicators.note: Two wrestlers grapple until neither is where he started, and letters put through that end up thoroughly out of position.

blocks.note: seven letters between those two words, exactly the seven the entry needs

explanation.surface: A mud-wrestling bout, stripped off, laid on for the holidaymakers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrestling in' reads as a single phrase and only the first word of it is the instruction — the 'in' belongs to the definition that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Bermuda is a British island group in the North Atlantic that lives largely on the holidaymakers its beaches bring in.

clue.text: Activity in church reminding you of something?

blocks.note: the tower team hauling on ropes, a Sunday morning sound in every English village
the idiom for a faint memory: something sounds faintly at the back of the mind and you half recognise it

explanation.surface: A churchgoer being asked whether the sound stirs a memory.
explanation.walkthrough: The same hyphenated word is defined twice, the second time through the idiom — a thing that rings a bell brings a memory back. Only the question mark warns that the second reading is playing.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the church-tower activity of sounding the bells, and the idiom 'that rings a bell' makes the same words mean jogging a memory.

clue.text: As a rule, what's found in an extremity of neoliberalism

definitions.note: The definition is adverbial where the answer is a noun: what happens as a rule is the thing the answer names, the standard case.

indicators.note: An extremity is an end, so this asks for a letter off one end of the word that follows, and 'an' declines to say which end.

blocks.note: the letter standing at the front end of that long word
only one extremity is asked for, either of them, and the little word that offers a choice between two things is spelt out in full
the letter standing at the other end of the same word

explanation.surface: The far edge of free-market politics, and what turns up out there.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'an extremity' politically and the clue is about where an ideology ends up. The joke is that the wordplay refuses to choose which end it means and writes that refusal into the middle of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The norm is what usually happens: the standard, the thing that holds as a rule rather than by exception.

clue.text: Describing ears somewhat idiotically

indicators.note: Somewhat means partly, so only a part of the word after it is wanted — a run of its letters rather than anything it means.

blocks.note: four letters in a row, sitting well inside that long adverb

explanation.surface: A silly way of talking about ears.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place is one long word rather than a run across a join, which is much harder to spot: no capital, no odd punctuation, and 'somewhat' reads as a throwaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Otic is the medical adjective for the ear, from the Greek — the root behind otitis and the label on ear drops.

clue.text: Beefy broth and duck, served badly, spoil a tux

indicators.note: A dish served badly arrives at the table in a state, and letters in that state are not in the order they were given.

blocks.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, written as a nought on the scorecard
nine letters taken exactly as they stand, for their spelling and not their sense

explanation.surface: A badly served dinner of broth and duck ends up down the front of a dinner jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: The menu is the disguise: 'and duck' reads as the second course and is really one letter off a cricket scorecard. Everything after the comma is raw material, the tux included.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxtail soup is made by simmering the tail of a bullock, so it is beef broth in the most literal way the butcher allows.

clue.text: Further some characters in Royal Society

indicators.note: Characters are letters as well as people, and 'some' of them means a run taken out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: four letters in a row that begin inside the first word and finish inside the second

explanation.surface: Advancing the careers of one or two figures at the Royal Society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Further' is a verb on the surface — to advance somebody's career — and an adverb in the answer. The Royal Society is Britain's national academy of science, here only for the letters at the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Also means in addition, which is the sense of 'further' when it introduces one more point rather than a greater distance.

clue.text: Balkan spice introduced to academic Scotsman

indicators.note: To introduce one person to another is to bring them face to face, so the piece named first is set against the ones named after it.

blocks.note: mace is the spice made from the lacy coat around a nutmeg
a don is a senior member of an Oxford or Cambridge college
Ian is the Scottish forename crosswords keep permanently on hand

explanation.surface: Someone presenting a jar of spice to a Scottish academic.
explanation.walkthrough: Three ordinary things are named and not one of them is Balkan; the definition is the single word at the front, an adjective standing in for a nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: Macedonian is the adjective for Macedonia, one of the countries of the Balkan peninsula, so it names one particular Balkan people.

clue.text: Workshy Everyman had leave (on vacation)

indicators.note: A vacated word has been emptied out, so only the letters standing at its two ends are left behind.

blocks.note: the setter signs himself Everyman, so this is 'I had' written short
the first and last letters of the word, with the middle emptied out

explanation.surface: A lazy setter who has just been away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyman' is the setter's own pen name, so it stands in for the first person: what Everyman had, I had. The bracketed phrase is holiday talk and an instruction at the same time.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody idle is doing no work, which is what 'workshy' accuses them of — the difference is only whether the laziness is deliberate.
